quartiers:Cidade Velha.name: Cidade Velha
quartiers:Cidade Velha.teaser: Fifteen minutes from gate to gate: orange trees, a bishop's palace and two cooks inside the old walls
quartiers:Cidade Velha.story: Walk in under the Arco da Vila and the noise of the Baixa drops away. The cobbles climb to the Largo da Sé, a square planted with orange trees, closed on one side by the cathedral and on another by the long front of the Paço Episcopal, the bishops' palace. Lanes run off to the old Convento da Assunção, now the city museum, and to the Galeria Trem, a former military warehouse showing contemporary art for free. Leave by the Arco do Repouso, the eastern gate with a 15th-century Our Lady of Rest above it, and the ramparts give onto salt marsh and lagoon.
quartiers:Cidade Velha.why: Stay for dinner: after the day visitors leave, the walled town goes quiet and the two best tables inside it fill up.

quartiers:The Baixa and Rua de Santo Ant.teaser: Black-and-white calçada underfoot, a 1908 café, a 1953 pastry counter and the city market one block over
quartiers:The Baixa and Rua de Santo Ant.story: North of the marina the old walls give way to the town Faro actually lives in. Rua de Santo António, pedestrian and paved in black-and-white limestone calçada, is lined with shops and pastry counters; mid-morning it smells of coffee and warm sugar from Gardy, open since 1953. Café Aliança, older still (1908), anchors the square at the bottom. A short walk east brings you to the Mercado Municipal and its fish slabs, and to the Largo do Carmo, where the Igreja do Carmo keeps its chapel of bones.

quartiers:The marina and the Jardim.name: The marina and the Jardim
quartiers:The marina and the Jardim.teaser: A small dock of fishing and pleasure boats, a garden facing the lagoon, and trains rolling past the water
quartiers:The marina and the Jardim.story: Faro's doca is small enough to take in at one look: pleasure boats and a few working hulls in a basin behind the railway, which runs along the waterfront so that the Algarve line's trains pass between the town and the salt marsh. At the head of the basin lies the Jardim Manuel Bívar, its bandstand and benches looking west over the water. Walk south along the walls to the Cais das Portas do Mar, where the island boats leave for Ilha Deserta, Culatra and the Farol, and the Centro Ciência Viva, whose roof terrace looks out over the Ria Formosa.

quartiers:Praia de Faro.name: Praia de Faro
quartiers:Praia de Faro.teaser: Faro's own Atlantic beach on a sand spit, with airliners sliding in low over the dunes
quartiers:Praia de Faro.story: Faro's ocean beach sits on the Ilha de Faro, a thin barrier spit about 7 km west of the centre, reached by a bridge over the lagoon channel next to the airport. Postal do Algarve reports that a new two-way bridge has replaced the old single-lane crossing. On the spit a road runs past houses, campsites, beach bars and grilled-fish restaurants: Atlantic surf on one side, the calm Ria Formosa on the other. Aircraft on approach to Faro airport pass low overhead, close enough to read the livery. In late October the summer crowd has gone; some beach restaurants cut their hours or close for winter.

curiosities:Portugal's first printed boo.name: Portugal's first printed book
curiosities:Portugal's first printed boo.teaser: Printing in Portugal began in Faro in 1487, in Hebrew, nine years before the Jews were expelled
curiosities:Portugal's first printed boo.story: Ask where Portuguese printing began and most people say Lisbon or Coimbra. The answer is Faro, and the language is Hebrew. On 30 June 1487 the press of Don Samuel Gacon finished a Pentateuch, the five books of Moses, set in square Hebrew letters with vowel points. One copy survives. It passed through Jewish hands in 16th-century Mantua, then the Almanzi collection in Padua, and reached the British Museum in the 1860s; it is now at the British Library. In December 1496 King Manuel I ordered the Jews out of Portugal, and Faro's press fell silent. In 2017, 530 years on, a facsimile was launched in Faro.
curiosities:Portugal's first printed boo.why: It turns the usual story upside down: the first book printed in Portugal was not in Portuguese and not printed in the capital.
facts: The Centro Histórico Judaico de Faro, with the Jewish cemetery of a later community and the Isaac Bitton museum, on Rua Leão Penedo by the hospital; listed open weekdays 09:30-12:30 and 14:00-17:00 (Oct 2026 listings): phone ahead. The book itself is in London, at the British Library

A 2004 auction catalogue suggests the press belonged to Don Samuel Porteiro, with Gacon as backer. And 'first book printed in Portugal' is not 'first book in Portuguese': that title usually goes to the Tratado de Confissom, printed at Chaves in 1489, itself debated

curiosities:The bishop's library at Oxfo.name: The bishop's library at Oxford
curiosities:The bishop's library at Oxfo.teaser: Essex sacked Faro in 1596 and carried off the bishop's books; they ended up on the Bodleian's first shelves
curiosities:The bishop's library at Oxfo.story: In July 1596, returning from the raid on Cádiz, the Earl of Essex landed at Faro and burned it. Among the loot was the library of the bishop, Fernando Martins Mascarenhas: Latin theology and law, many volumes stamped with his arms on the binding. Essex gave the books to his friend Thomas Bodley, who was restocking Oxford's university library, and they sat among the first books when the Bodleian opened in 1602. They are still there; some have been digitised and can be paged through online. In Faro, the Faro 1540 association keeps asking for them back.
curiosities:The bishop's library at Oxfo.why: Few cities can point to their own stolen library on the founding shelves of one of the world's great libraries.
facts: The Paço Episcopal, the bishops' palace on the Largo da Sé, from the outside; the books themselves on Digital Bodleian

curiosities:Tempura went from here.name: Tempura went from here
curiosities:Tempura went from here.teaser: Japan's tempura may carry a Portuguese word in its name: whose word, and which one, is still argued
curiosities:Tempura went from here.story: Portuguese ships reached Japan in the 1540s; Jesuits and traders stayed until 1639. The story told in every Portuguese tasca is that they brought frying in batter with them. On the têmporas, the Ember days of the church calendar, Catholics went without meat and ate fried vegetables and fish instead; the Japanese, the story goes, heard the word and kept it as tempura. The Portuguese dish usually named as the ancestor is peixinhos da horta, 'little fish from the garden': green beans dipped in batter and fried. A good story with a real core: the Portuguese presence is certain, the exact route is not.
curiosities:Tempura went from here.why: Order peixinhos da horta in Faro and taste the argument for yourself: thin batter, a green bean, a little salt.
facts: Peixinhos da horta on the petiscos list of a Faro tasca; the dish itself is The Dish's card

Têmpora (Ember days, Latin tempora) is the most cited source of the word; tempero or temperar (seasoning, to season) is the main rival, and some say the question cannot be settled. The link to peixinhos da horta specifically is popular but thinly documented

curiosities:The storks of the Arco.name: The storks of the Arco
curiosities:The storks of the Arco.teaser: An 1812 arch, an Arab horseshoe door inside it, and storks that have stopped flying to Africa
curiosities:The storks of the Arco.story: Look up at the old town gate: a white stork stands on an enormous nest on top of the Arco da Vila. The neoclassical arch below was opened in 1812, commissioned by Bishop Francisco Gomes do Avelar from Francisco Xavier Fabri, the Italian architect who rebuilt much of the Algarve after 1755; a marble Saint Thomas Aquinas stands in its niche. Walk through and you meet the older gate behind it, a horseshoe-arched door of Arab origin, beside a niche recalling a Marian miracle legend. The storks were once summer visitors; since the mid-1980s more and more stay all winter, some on their nests in December.
curiosities:The storks of the Arco.why: Stand in the passage and look both ways: neoclassical marble on the town side, the Islamic gate within, and a stork above both.
facts: Walk through the Arco da Vila from Rua da Misericórdia into the old town; free, open all the time

How old the horseshoe door is. The old guide calls it 11th-century; the Islamic albarrã towers by the gate are dated to the 11th century, and the Arab walls to the 9th to 11th centuries, but no source we found dates the door itself. Fabri is called Genoese in some sources, simply Italian in others

culture:The Sé and its tower.name: The Sé and its tower
culture:The Sé and its tower.teaser: A cathedral on a Roman temple, a 1715 German-school organ, and the lagoon from the tower
culture:The Sé and its tower.story: The Sé stands where a Roman temple, a Visigothic church and a mosque stood before it; after Afonso III took Faro in 1249 the mosque was turned into a church. English raiders burned it in 1596 and much of what you see is later. Inside, the eye goes to the organ: built in 1715 by Johann Heinrich Hulenkampf, a pupil of the Hamburg master Arp Schnitger, enlarged after the 1767 earthquake and restored by Flentrop in 1974. Then climb the narrow stair of the tower. From the top the whole Ria Formosa lays itself out: salt pans, the barrier islands, Culatra's fishing village, the Atlantic beyond.
culture:The Sé and its tower.why: Go up the tower at opening, before the groups: it is the clearest map of the lagoon you will get anywhere.

culture:Museu Municipal.name: Museu Municipal
culture:Museu Municipal.teaser: A Roman sea god's mosaic face in the chapter rooms of a convent founded by a queen in 1519
culture:Museu Municipal.story: Two nuns from Beja began this convent in 1519 with the backing of Queen Leonor, then lady of Faro; a decade later Queen Catarina paid for a second phase, and master Afonso Pires built the cloister, finished in 1548 and counted among the first Renaissance cloisters in Portugal. Arcades round a central well: at four in the afternoon the stone is warm and the place is silent. The municipal museum, founded in 1894, moved in during 1973. Its star is the Roman Mosaic of the Ocean, a 3rd-century floor found in Faro in 1976, the sea god's face looking up from the floor.

culture:Capela dos Ossos.name: Capela dos Ossos
culture:Capela dos Ossos.teaser: A small chapel lined with the skulls of Carmelite friars, and a sentence addressed straight at you
culture:Capela dos Ossos.story: Walk through the gilded Baroque church of the Carmo and out the back to a room about four metres by six. Its walls and vault are built of bones: skulls in rows, thigh bones laid in patterns, taken from the friars' old cemetery when it was cleared. The chapel was consecrated in 1816, and the count usually given is 1,245 skulls, from more than a thousand friars. Over the door, in Portuguese rather than Latin, it speaks to you directly: «Pára aqui a considerar que a este estado hás-de chegar», 'Stop here and consider that you will come to this state.'

culture:Teatro Lethes.name: Teatro Lethes
culture:Teatro Lethes.teaser: A Jesuit college turned into a velvet horseshoe theatre by a Venetian doctor, open again for autumn
culture:Teatro Lethes.story: Bishop Mascarenhas founded a Jesuit college here, licensed in 1599 and finished early in the next century. The Jesuits were expelled in 1759, Napoleon's troops later camped inside, and in 1843 the building went at auction to Lázaro Doglioni, a doctor from Venice who wanted a theatre on the lines of Lisbon's São Carlos and La Scala. It opened on 4 April 1845, Queen Maria II's birthday, with the motto «monet oblectando», it teaches by delighting. Inside: tiers of boxes in a horseshoe, red plush, a stage close enough to hear breathing. Storm damage to the stage stopped shows last winter; the season resumed in September 2026.

culture:Milreu.name: Milreu
culture:Milreu.teaser: A Roman villa at Estói with fish swimming across its bath floors and a temple to the waters
culture:Milreu.story: Ten kilometres inland from Faro, at the edge of Estói, lie the ruins of a large Roman country house that stood near Ossonoba, the Roman town beneath Faro. Walk it in the morning with nobody else there, then go up into the village, where the pink Palácio de Estói rises above its gardens.

provisioning:Flor de sal de Tavira.name: Flor de sal de Tavira
provisioning:Flor de sal de Tavira.teaser: The thin top crust of the Tavira salt pans, raked off by hand in summer and sold with a DOP seal
provisioning:Flor de sal de Tavira.story: Flor de sal is the fragile skin of crystals that forms on the brine of the Ria Formosa salt pans on hot, still, dry days. Salt workers lift it off by hand between June and September with the borboleta, a butterfly-shaped wooden tool, then leave it to dry in the sun. Nothing is washed, refined or added, and the flakes crumble between the fingers. The salt of Tavira has a long paper trail: the old guide dates the Crown's claim on its salinas to Afonso III in 1266. Scatter it at the end, on grilled fish or a sliced tomato, never into the cooking water.

walks:The Ludo trail and the salt pans.name: The Ludo trail and the salt pans
walks:The Ludo trail and the salt pans.teaser: A flat lagoon loop past salt pans where the flamingo flocks grow from October to March
walks:The Ludo trail and the salt pans.story: The Caminho do Ludo runs flat through the western end of the Ria Formosa natural park, created in 1987: brackish lagoons, pine and eucalyptus, the São Lourenço wetland, then the square mirrors of the salt pans. A few greater flamingos stay all year, but the big flocks are here from October to March, so late autumn is the right moment. Look for spoonbills, avocets and godwits working the mud. avoid:Jet-skis in the lagoon.story: The Ria Formosa has been a Natural Park since 9 December 1987, when Decree-Law 373/87 upgraded the 1978 nature reserve. craft:What is sold as Algarve craft.teaser: A shiny copper cataplana at a souvenir price did not come off a Loulé bench
craft:What is sold as Algarve craft.story: The souvenir shops between the marina and Rua de Santo António sell copper cataplanas by the shelf. Hand-hammered ones are slow and few: Analide Carmo in Loulé needs about three days for one, and a 20 cm pot from his bench was quoted at about €100. When a resort in Albufeira wanted a giant cataplana, its organiser said copper is no longer worked at that scale in the Algarve and ordered it from makers in the north of Portugal. A pot that is perfectly smooth, cheap and stacked by the dozen was made in a factory. Ask the shop who made it and where; a real maker has a name.
craft:What is sold as Algarve craft.why: Buy the copper in Loulé and the palm weaving from the women who plait it.
facts: Turn the pot over: hand work shows hammer marks and riveted hinges, factory pieces are mirror-smooth and identical. Ask for the maker's name and town

linger:Café Aliança.name: Café Aliança
linger:Café Aliança.teaser: A café open since 1908 on the marina square, where Faro argued politics and wrote poetry
linger:Café Aliança.story: Aliança opened in 1908 by the marina, and the press still calls it one of the oldest cafés in Portugal (Postal says third oldest). Inside: a revolving door, dark wood panelling, copper over the counter, and on the walls the faces that sat here, Simone de Beauvoir among them, and the Algarve poet António Aleixo. Faro's mayor called it the room where people talked politics and art and wrote poetry and prose. It has closed and reopened several times since 2009; the CTT put it on a stamp in 2017, and it reopened in October 2023 under new management as café, restaurant and bar.
linger:Café Aliança.why: Take a coffee at the counter under the old photographs, then walk out onto the square facing the boats.

linger:Pastelaria Gardy.story: Gardy has stood on Rua de Santo António, the white-paved shopping street of the Baixa, since 1953. You come in under brick arches to long glass counters: custard tarts, the little almond and fig sweets of the Algarve, carob cakes, the layered folhados of Tavira and Dom Rodrigo in its twist of foil. Locals stand at the bar for a bica and a pastel de nata; outside, shoppers take a table and a fresh Algarve orange juice. It is a place for the regional sweets in one stop, not a quiet room.

linger:Jardim Manuel Bívar.teaser: Palms, a bandstand and benches looking west over the marina to the lagoon
linger:Jardim Manuel Bívar.story: The garden fills the strip of land between the Baixa and the little marina, with the walls of the Cidade Velha and the Arco da Vila at its southern end. It is a 19th-century public garden: tall palms, shaded benches and, at its heart, the iron bandstand that the city restored in 2023 as an emblem of the lower town. The tour boats for the islands load at the quay a few steps away. Toward evening the light drops behind the lagoon and the marshes of the Ria Formosa turn copper.

drink:Negra Mole.name: Negra Mole
drink:Negra Mole.teaser: An old grape with pink, red and black berries on one bunch, poured pale, almost as a rosé
drink:Negra Mole.story: Negra Mole is the grape the Algarve kept. The regional wine commission calls it the second-oldest Portuguese variety after Sercial, and its bunches ripen unevenly, pink, red and near-black berries side by side. That gives a pale, low-tannin wine of fresh red fruit, the old palhete and clarete of Algarve tables. In the late 20th century it disappeared into anonymous blends, and many vineyards were pulled up for resorts and golf. From about 2010 growers began bottling it alone again, now as light reds, rosés and traditional-method sparklers: Cabrita in Silves makes a blanc de noirs and a rosé from it, Morgado do Quintão an espumante.
drink:Negra Mole.why: Ask for it slightly cool with grilled fish: it is the red that does not fight the sea.
facts: Pale ruby, red cherry and strawberry, light tannin; sparkling versions are white or pale pink

drink:Arinto.name: Arinto
drink:Arinto.teaser: The white that stays sharp in the southern heat: lemon, green apple, a mineral finish
drink:Arinto.story: Arinto is grown all over Portugal for one reason: it holds its acidity when the sun does its worst. In the Algarve it is the backbone of most serious white blends and is also bottled alone. Young, it tastes of lemon, lime and green apple with a stony finish; some producers ferment or age it in barrel, which rounds it without losing the edge. That bite is what you want against a cataplana or a plate of clams, where butter, oil and lagoon brine need something to cut them.
drink:Arinto.why: The safe white order at any Algarve table where shellfish is coming.
facts: Pale lemon, citrus and green apple, high acidity, a mineral finish

drink:Crato Branco.name: Crato Branco
drink:Crato Branco.teaser: The Algarve's own name for Síria, a softer, more aromatic white than Arinto
drink:Crato Branco.story: Order Crato Branco in Faro and you are drinking a grape that changes its name at every provincial border: Síria is its official Portuguese name, Roupeiro in the Alentejo, Códega in the Douro, Crato Branco here. It ripens late and gives a fragrant white, ripe stone fruit and flowers, rounder and softer than Arinto, so the two are often blended. Its history in the Algarve is long: José André Cabrita planted it at Quinta da Vinha, near Silves, in 1977, and Morgado do Quintão bottles it on its own.
drink:Crato Branco.why: Drink it with grilled fish or a sea bream baked in salt, where Arinto would be too sharp.
facts: Pale gold, peach, melon and flowers, softer acidity than Arinto

drink:Medronho.name: Medronho
drink:Medronho.teaser: Clear and strong, distilled from the wild red berries of the strawberry tree in the Monchique hills
drink:Medronho.story: The strawberry tree, medronheiro, grows wild on the schist hills of the Serra de Monchique, and in autumn its round berries turn from yellow to deep red. Families pick them, leave them to ferment for weeks, about two months for one Monchique maker, then distil the mash in copper stills over the winter, often into February and March. The result is clear, very strong and smells of ripe fruit and the hillside; aged in wood, it turns gold. The old guide, citing DGADR, gives it a protected name, Medronho do Algarve IGP; the regional wine commission was named its certifier in 2016. The still itself: see Casa do Medronho.
drink:Medronho.why: A small glass after coffee, at room temperature, in a tasca that buys from a hill family.
facts: Clear (gold if aged), ripe red fruit and earth; very strong, often close to 50% (the old guide said about 48%)

drink:Bagaceira.name: Bagaceira
drink:Bagaceira.teaser: Portugal's grape-skin brandy, the cousin of grappa, poured after a long lunch
drink:Bagaceira.story: When the wine is pressed, the skins, pips and stalks left behind are not wasted: they are distilled into bagaceira, Portugal's answer to marc and grappa. Young, it is clear, hot and grapey; aged in oak as bagaceira velha it turns amber and softer. It is made across the country, and the Algarve has no protected name of its own, but some cellars distil the pomace of their own grapes, Negra Mole and Castelão among them. Ask at a winery tasting whether they have one.
drink:Bagaceira.why: Ask for it when medronho is too fierce: same ritual, a grape-skin taste.
facts: Clear and fiery young; amber, softer and woodier when aged

bars:Bago Wine Bar.name: Bago Wine Bar
bars:Bago Wine Bar.teaser: A small Baixa wine bar run by Rui Martins, with Portuguese and natural wines open by the glass
bars:Bago Wine Bar.story: Bago is on a quiet side street in the Baixa, with a few tables on the terrace and shelves of bottles inside. Its owner, Rui Martins, buys Portuguese wine, much of it natural, organic or biodynamic, and keeps about ten bottles open to pour by the glass, so you can taste an Algarve Negra Mole beside something from the Douro or Bairrada. Small plates come with it: cheese, charcuterie, toasts, roast black-pork sausage. It is listed on Raisin, the natural-wine guide, and on Friday evenings there has often been live music.

bars:The Hotel Faro rooftop.story: The Cosmopolitan bar sits on the fifth-floor roof of Hotel Faro, on the square at the head of the marina. It faces west, so from the terrace you look over the masts and the Jardim Manuel Bívar to the marshes of the Ria Formosa and the line of the barrier islands. The cocktails are named after airlines; the crowd is hotel guests and visitors in for the view, and the music is occasional. It is not a bargain, and the view is what you are paying for.
